title: Website, Google Ads and local SEO for a Harare solar installer
summary: How we would help a Harare solar installer turn searches for backup power into booked site assessments, with a fast website, tightly managed Google Ads and a stronger presence on Google Maps.

mock.label: Solar · Harare
mock.headline: Solar that keeps your home running

brief: In this example, the business is an established solar installer in Harare. It designs and fits inverter and battery backup systems, full rooftop installations and solar borehole pumps for homes and small businesses. Most of its work comes from referrals, and its website is an old brochure site that few people find. The owner wants a steady flow of serious enquiries from Harare's suburbs and nearby towns such as Chitungwiza, Ruwa and Norton. Some enquiries come from Zimbabweans abroad who are paying for a system at a family home.
challenge: Solar is a big purchase, and Harare buyers have plenty of choice: established installers, hardware shops, importers and one-person operators on Facebook. Many people have heard stories of batteries that failed early or systems that were sized badly, so trust counts for more than the lowest price. Searches range from people ready to book an assessment to people comparing inverter prices or hunting for spare parts. Paying for the wrong clicks gets expensive quickly. Demand also rises and falls with the power situation, so the plan has to work in busy and quiet spells alike.
approach: Research how Harare buys solar

We would map the searches people make, from installer searches in Harare to questions about battery sizes and keeping a fridge and lights on, and sort them by buying intent. We would also confirm which areas the business covers, from Borrowdale to Waterfalls, and how competitors present their packages.
Build a website that sells systems, not parts

We would build a fast, mobile-first site with clear package pages for homes, businesses and borehole pumps. It would include a plain guide to what each system can run, photos of real installations and straight answers on warranties and after-sales support. Every page would carry click-to-call, a WhatsApp button and a short quote form that asks which appliances the customer wants to power.
Run Google Ads on high-intent searches

Search campaigns would target people ready to speak to an installer, only in the areas the business serves. Negative keywords would filter out job seekers, DIY shoppers and spare-part hunters. A small test campaign would reach Zimbabweans in the UK and South Africa buying for family homes. Calls, WhatsApp clicks and forms would all be tracked, so budget follows the searches that lead to site assessments.
Show up on Google Maps

We would complete the Google Business Profile with the right categories, service areas, products and photos of finished jobs, and set up a simple routine for asking every customer for a review once their system is running. Consistent listings on local directories would back this up.
deliverables: Mobile-first website with package, service-area and FAQ pages
Quote form that captures the appliances each customer wants to power
Google Ads search campaigns, plus a diaspora test campaign
Optimised Google Business Profile and a review request routine
GA4 and Google Tag Manager tracking for calls, WhatsApp clicks and forms
Monthly dashboard and a plain-English review call
measure: Quote requests by channel: calls, WhatsApp and forms
Cost per qualified quote request from Google Ads
Share of enquiries that become site assessments and installations
Map visibility for installer searches across the target suburbs
Number and recency of genuine Google reviews
description: Example project: how we would win more solar quote requests in Harare with a faster website, Google Ads and a stronger Google Maps listing.

title: Enrolment campaign for a private school in Bulawayo
summary: How we would help an independent school in Bulawayo fill places for the January intake, with Meta ads timed around open days, focused landing pages and quick, friendly follow-up on WhatsApp.

mock.label: School · Bulawayo
mock.headline: Now enrolling for the January intake

brief: In this example, the business is an independent co-educational day school in one of Bulawayo's low-density suburbs, running from ECD through primary to A Level, with Cambridge and ZIMSEC pathways. Most new families find it through word of mouth. Enquiries arrive by phone, Facebook message and WhatsApp, and a busy admissions office answers them when it can. The head wants more enquiries from the right families before the January intake, fuller open days and a clear view of where each new pupil came from.
challenge: Choosing a school is a big decision, and fees are a long-term commitment, so parents compare several schools and take their time. Many Bulawayo families have a parent working in South Africa, so the person paying the fees may not be in Bulawayo at all. Enrolment also runs to a fixed calendar. Ads that start late miss the families who decided weeks earlier. And when a WhatsApp enquiry waits days for a reply, the parent has often moved on to the next school.
approach: Learn how parents choose

We would start with video calls with the head and the admissions team, and list the questions parents ask most, from fees and class sizes to transport and sport. Then we would map the enrolment calendar: open days, assessment dates and application deadlines for each entry point.
Build a landing page for each entry point

We would create separate, fast-loading pages for ECD, Grade 1, Form 1 and A Level entry. Each would answer parents' real questions and include a short video tour, an open day booking form and a WhatsApp button. Fees would be shown the way the school prefers, on the page or sent on request.
Run Meta ads around the calendar

Facebook and Instagram campaigns would reach parents in and around Bulawayo, using photos and short videos filmed on a school visit arranged with the head. Pupils would appear only with their parents' consent. Ads would run in English, with Ndebele versions tested alongside. A smaller campaign would reach Bulawayo families living in South Africa, and retargeting would remind parents who viewed a page but did not book.
Follow up every enquiry on WhatsApp

We would set up WhatsApp Business with a greeting, quick replies and labels for each stage, plus a simple sequence: prospectus, open day reminder, application form, assessment date. Every enquiry would go into one tracker, so the admissions office can see who is waiting and nobody goes unanswered.
deliverables: A landing page for each entry point, with open day booking
Meta campaigns with video, carousel and lead ads, planned around the intake calendar
Click-to-WhatsApp ads and a WhatsApp Business set-up with quick replies and labels
Follow-up messages for prospectus requests, open day reminders and application steps
Enquiry tracker for the admissions office, with a weekly summary
Tracking for open day bookings, WhatsApp chats and applications
measure: Enquiries by entry point and by channel
Cost per open day booking
Time to first reply on WhatsApp enquiries
Enquiries that go on to applications and assessments
Applications that become confirmed places
description: Example project: how we would help a Bulawayo private school fill its January intake with Meta ads, intake pages and fast WhatsApp follow-up.

title: Direct bookings for a lodge near Victoria Falls
summary: How we would help a small lodge near Victoria Falls win more direct bookings, with a booking-ready website, clear answers for AI search, proper tracking and ads aimed at travellers abroad and Zimbabweans visiting home.

mock.label: Victoria Falls lodge
mock.headline: Wake up near the Smoke that Thunders

brief: In this example, the business is a family-run lodge with a handful of chalets on the edge of Victoria Falls town, close to the Zambezi National Park. Guests come for the falls, river cruises and game drives, and for a quieter stay away from the town centre. Most bookings arrive through online travel agencies and tour operators, so the lodge pays commission on almost every night it sells. The owners want more guests to book direct on the lodge's own website, and they want to know which marketing brings those bookings in.
challenge: International travellers plan months ahead, compare many options on booking sites and read reviews closely, so a small lodge has to look trustworthy at every step. Many know little about travelling in Zimbabwe and want clear answers on transfers, payments and what to expect. The booking engine runs on a separate system, so tracking often breaks between the website and the booking, and nobody can see which channel earned the sale. Travellers are also starting to ask AI assistants where to stay, and those answers lean on places whose details are clear and consistent across the web.
approach: Fix the tracking first

We would set up GA4 and Google Tag Manager with cross-domain tracking to the booking engine, so every direct booking is recorded with its value and source. That would give an honest starting point for comparing direct bookings with those from agencies.
Make the website the easiest place to book

We would build a fast, mobile-first site with clear room pages, rates and inclusions, a getting-here guide and the booking engine one tap away on every page. Any perks for booking direct, such as flexible dates or airport transfers, would be stated plainly. Honest photos and video would be shot on a visit arranged with the owners.
Become a clear answer for AI and search

We would write question-led pages on getting to the falls, transfers, activities and how the falls change between high and low water. We would add lodging schema and match the lodge's details across Google Business Profile, Tripadvisor and booking sites. Each month we would check how ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot and Perplexity answer a fixed set of travel questions.
Advertise to people already planning a trip

Google search ads would cover Victoria Falls accommodation searches and the lodge's own name, so booking sites do not catch people already looking for it. Meta ads would reach travellers in the UK, the US and South Africa, and Zimbabweans abroad planning a family holiday back home. Retargeting would remind visitors who checked dates but did not book.
deliverables: Mobile-first website with room, activity and getting-here pages
Booking engine integration with cross-domain tracking and booking values in GA4
Data Studio dashboard comparing direct and agency bookings
Question-led content, lodging schema and consistent listings across the web
Google and Meta campaigns for international, regional and diaspora travellers
Monthly AI answer checks across ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot and Perplexity
measure: Direct bookings and booking value, compared with agency bookings
Website booking conversion rate by country
Cost per direct booking from paid campaigns
How often the lodge is named in AI answers to travel questions
Visits from organic search and AI assistants
description: Example project: how we would grow direct bookings for a Victoria Falls lodge with a booking-ready website, AEO, GA4 tracking and targeted ads.

title: E-commerce, email and WhatsApp automation for a diaspora grocery store
summary: How we would help a Harare online grocery and hamper store earn the trust of Zimbabweans abroad, with an easy store, clear delivery information, and email and WhatsApp messages that encourage buyers to come back each month.

mock.label: Groceries · Diaspora
mock.headline: Send groceries home from wherever you are

brief: In this example, the business is a Harare-based online store that lets Zimbabweans abroad buy groceries and hampers for family at home. It sells mealie-meal, cooking oil, rice, meat packs and toiletries, plus festive and back-to-school hampers. It delivers across Harare and Chitungwiza, and to other towns by courier. Orders currently come in on WhatsApp and are paid by bank transfer, which means hours of admin and lost sales. The owners want a proper online store, a quick checkout for buyers in the UK, South Africa, the US and Australia, and a way to turn first orders into regular monthly ones.
challenge: The person paying and the person receiving are far apart, so trust is everything. Buyers need to know the order will arrive, in good condition, at the right house. Checkout has to work with cards from banks abroad, while family at home may want to pay for extras with mobile money. Buyers live in different time zones, from the UK to Australia, so messages sent on Harare time can land in the middle of the night. And competition is strong, from established diaspora services and from simply sending cash.
approach: Build a store buyers abroad can trust

We would build a mobile-first store with real photos of every hamper, clear US dollar prices, and delivery towns and timings set out plainly. Buyers could save an address book of the relatives they send to. Checkout would accept international cards, with local options such as mobile money for orders placed in Zimbabwe.
Show every order arriving

WhatsApp messages would keep buyers updated from order confirmation to packing and delivery, ending with a delivery photo where the recipient is happy to have one taken. Clear substitution rules and a quick way to reach a real person on WhatsApp would answer the questions that cause the most worry.
Automate the follow-up

We would set up email and WhatsApp flows for welcome messages, abandoned carts, post-purchase thanks and monthly restock reminders, all sent at sensible hours in each buyer's time zone. Seasonal campaigns would be planned well ahead for Christmas, Easter and the start of the school year.
Reach Zimbabweans abroad

Google search and Meta catalogue ads would reach shoppers in South Africa, the UK, the US and Australia who buy for family in Zimbabwe, with retargeting for people who browsed but did not buy. Sales would be tracked in GA4 by buyer country, so budget goes to the markets where first orders turn into repeat customers.
deliverables: Mobile-first online store with hamper bundles, delivery zones and a recipient address book
International card checkout, with mobile money for buyers in Zimbabwe
Email flows for welcome, abandoned carts, post-purchase and monthly restock reminders
WhatsApp order updates from confirmation to delivery
Product feed for Meta catalogue ads, plus Google search campaigns for each buyer country
GA4 e-commerce tracking with revenue by buyer country
measure: Orders and revenue by buyer country
Checkout completion rate
Repeat purchase rate and time between orders
Revenue from email and WhatsApp flows
Cost to win a first order, against the value of repeat orders
description: Example project: an online grocery and hamper store for Zimbabweans abroad, with a trusted checkout, delivery updates and WhatsApp automation.

title: Local SEO and farming content for an agricultural supplier in Mutare
summary: How we would help a Mutare farm supplies business get found by farmers across Manicaland, through a stronger Google Business Profile, local search pages and practical seasonal guides in English and Shona.

mock.label: Agriculture · Mutare
mock.headline: Seed, fertiliser and advice for Manicaland farmers

brief: In this example, the business is an established agricultural supplier in Mutare. It sells seed, fertiliser, crop chemicals, irrigation fittings, stockfeed and small equipment, and has an agronomist on hand to advise customers. Its customers range from smallholders around Mutare to commercial growers further afield in Manicaland. It has a basic website and a Google Business Profile that nobody has updated in years. The owner wants more farmers to find the shop when they search, to call or WhatsApp before travelling into town, and to see the business as a trusted source of advice.
challenge: Buying is seasonal. Demand peaks before the summer rains, when farmers stock up on seed and fertiliser, so much of the year's trade can fall into a few busy months. Farming in Manicaland is also very varied, from bananas in Burma Valley and potatoes in Nyanga to tea, coffee and macadamias around Chipinge, so one generic message will not fit everyone. Many farmers search on a phone with limited data, often in Shona. A trip into Mutare costs time and money, so they want to check prices and stock before they set off. Larger national chains compete for the same searches too.
approach: Fix the Google Business Profile

We would claim and complete the profile with the right categories, opening hours including seasonal changes, products and fresh photos of the shop and stock, taken on a visit arranged with the owner. Weekly posts would announce new arrivals, and a simple review request at the till and on WhatsApp would help build genuine reviews from farmers.
Build pages farmers actually search for

We would create product category pages for seed, fertiliser, crop chemicals, irrigation and stockfeed, plus pages for the farming areas the business serves, such as Odzi, Penhalonga, Burma Valley and Rusape. Each page would load quickly on mobile data and make calling or messaging on WhatsApp easy.
Publish practical seasonal guides

A content calendar would follow the farming year: land preparation, planting, top dressing, pest alerts such as fall armyworm, and winter crops. Short guides written with the shop's agronomist, in English and Shona, would be easy to share on WhatsApp and Facebook, and would give Google and AI tools clear, local answers to quote.
Keep listings consistent and measure what matters

We would correct the business name, address, phone number and hours across Zimbabwean directories and social profiles, and look for links from farming associations and local media. Calls, direction requests and WhatsApp chats would be tracked, so the owner can see each month what search brings in.
deliverables: Claimed and fully completed Google Business Profile, with products and weekly posts
Review request cards for the till and a WhatsApp review message
Product category and service-area pages for the farming areas served
Seasonal content calendar with guides in English and Shona
Listing clean-up across Zimbabwean directories and social profiles
Monthly local search report covering calls, directions and WhatsApp chats
measure: Calls, direction requests and website clicks from the Google Business Profile
Map visibility for key product searches in Mutare and nearby areas
Organic visits to product pages and seasonal guides
WhatsApp enquiries started from the website and profile
Genuine Google reviews gained each month
description: Example project: how we would help a Mutare farm supplier reach Manicaland farmers with local SEO, Google Business Profile and seasonal guides.

title: B2B lead generation and CRM for a Harare accounting firm
summary: How we would help a Harare accounting and tax firm win more of the right business clients, using LinkedIn and search campaigns, useful tax content and a CRM that follows every lead from first contact to signed engagement.

mock.label: Accountants · Harare
mock.headline: Clear numbers for growing Zimbabwean businesses

brief: In this example, the business is a mid-sized accounting and tax practice in Harare. It offers bookkeeping, payroll, tax compliance and advisory work to small and medium-sized companies. Almost all new clients come through referrals, which has served the firm well but makes growth hard to plan. The partners want a steady flow of enquiries from companies that match their ideal client, especially for outsourced accounting and tax advisory work, and they want to see which marketing turns into signed engagements.
challenge: Choosing an accountant is a high-trust decision that owners rarely rush, and many only start looking when something goes wrong: a ZIMRA query, a missed deadline or a difficult year-end. Decision-makers are busy and wary of cold approaches. LinkedIn's audience in Zimbabwe is relatively small, so targeting has to be precise and the same people should not see the same ads over and over. Marketing also has to stay factual and within the profession's ethical rules. And leads arrive by phone, email, WhatsApp and LinkedIn, so without a CRM they are hard to follow up and impossible to trace back to a channel.
approach: Define the ideal client and the triggers

We would work with the partners to pin down the most valuable services and client types. Then we would list the moments that send a company looking for a new accountant: a ZIMRA query, fast growth, a new finance system or a year-end that went badly. Messages and offers would be built around those moments.
Publish expertise people can use

We would produce a tax calendar covering QPDs (quarterly payment dates) and other key deadlines, plain-English summaries of tax changes after each national budget, and practical checklists for year-end and payroll. The checklists would be offered as downloads in exchange for contact details, and partners would share shorter versions on LinkedIn.
Run focused LinkedIn and search campaigns

After a check in Campaign Manager that Zimbabwe can be targeted and the audience is large enough, LinkedIn Sponsored Content and Lead Gen Forms would target owners, directors and finance managers at Zimbabwean companies of the right size, with budgets managed so the same people are not overloaded. Google search ads would catch people already looking for tax consultants or outsourced accounting in Harare.
Connect every lead to the CRM and to revenue

We would set up Pipedrive or HubSpot with stages from enquiry to proposal to signed engagement. Website forms, LinkedIn leads, calls and WhatsApp chats would all flow into it, with follow-up reminders for partners. GA4, the LinkedIn Insight Tag and offline conversion imports would show which channels lead to real fee income.
deliverables: Ideal client profile and messaging guide for each core service
Tax calendar landing page and downloadable checklists with lead capture
LinkedIn Lead Gen Form and Google Search campaigns
CRM set-up with pipeline stages, lead routing and follow-up reminders
GA4, LinkedIn Insight Tag and offline conversion tracking
Monthly dashboard of leads, proposals and pipeline value by channel
measure: Qualified leads by channel and service line
Cost per qualified lead and per proposal sent
Lead-to-meeting and meeting-to-engagement rates
Pipeline value created by each marketing channel
Time from first enquiry to first response
description: Example project: B2B lead generation for a Harare accounting firm with LinkedIn and Google Ads, useful tax content and a CRM for every lead.
